name: Song Dynasty

fields.foundation: The Song Dynasty was founded in 960 CE by Zhao Kuangyin, a military commander of the Later Zhou who seized power in the Chenqiao Mutiny, when his troops draped him in the imperial yellow robe and proclaimed him emperor. He is known by his temple name Taizu, and the dynasty he founded governed China for over three centuries in two phases. The Northern Song (960–1127) reunified most of the Chinese heartland after the fragmentation of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period. It never recovered the Sixteen Prefectures around modern Beijing, which the Khitan Liao dynasty held, and under the Chanyuan Treaty of 1005 it agreed to costly annual payments of silk and silver to the Liao. Taizu and his successor Taizong deliberately placed the military under civilian control, a response to the regional warlordism that had destroyed the Tang and produced the chaos that followed. They subordinated military commanders to civil officials and expanded the examination system to staff a broad bureaucracy chosen by merit. The dynasty's military weakness proved fatal when the Jurchen Jin captured the capital Kaifeng in 1127 and carried off the retired emperor Huizong and his son, the reigning emperor Qinzong. The Song court re-formed in the south as the Southern Song (1127–1279), with its capital eventually fixed at Lin'an (modern Hangzhou). Despite the loss of the north, the Southern Song sustained a population of perhaps 60 to 70 million and a commercial economy more developed than any Europe would have for centuries, and its culture was among the most accomplished of the medieval world.
fields.socioeconomy: The Song economy was the most commercially developed the world had yet seen, with widespread use of paper money, extensive domestic and maritime trade, proto-industrial production and an urban commercial culture that changed Chinese society. Kaifeng and Lin'an were among the largest cities in the world. Lin'an at its peak probably held more than a million inhabitants, served by restaurants, entertainment quarters, financial institutions and specialised craft workshops. Paper money, from the jiaozi of Sichuan, issued by the state from 1024, to the huizi of the Southern Song, allowed transactions on a scale impossible with copper coinage alone, and helped to join regional markets into a national commercial system. Maritime trade through Guangzhou, Quanzhou and Mingzhou brought in large customs revenues, collected by maritime trade superintendencies, and connected Song China to Southeast Asia, South Asia, the Persian Gulf and East Africa. Exports of silk, ceramics and tea went out in exchange for spices, aromatics, tropical woods and precious goods. Under Emperor Zhenzong, early-ripening, drought-tolerant Champa rice was introduced from central Vietnam; it allowed double cropping in southern China and supported the period's rapid population growth. Coal and iron production in the north, especially in Hebei and Shanxi, reached scales that Europe would not surpass until the eighteenth century. Payments to the Liao and Xi Xia, and later the Jin, and the cost of huge standing armies consumed a large share of state revenue. This set reformers against the conservative establishment. The best known reformer was Wang Anshi, whose New Policies of 1069 attempted structural fiscal reform; the conservatives later reversed many of his measures.
fields.military: The Song military was limited by the dynasty's founding decision to subordinate military power to civilian government, a choice that put domestic political stability before frontier security. The professional standing army, the Imperial Armies (jinjun), together with the prefectural forces (xiang jun), exceeded one million men by the mid-eleventh century, but it was notoriously ill-disciplined, poorly equipped and often directed by civil officials with little military experience. Cavalry was the chronic weakness. The dynasty never controlled the northern grasslands needed to breed warhorses in sufficient numbers, and so depended on infantry against mounted opponents who had decisive advantages in open terrain. New weapons partly made up for this: Song armies developed and used gunpowder weapons, including fire arrows, bombs and early fire lances, well before they appeared elsewhere, and the formula for gunpowder was first recorded in the military compendium Wujing Zongyao of 1044. The navy was the Southern Song's greatest military strength. Its standing navy, founded in 1132, and its Yangtze river fleets were among the most capable of the age and defeated the Jin at Tangdao and Caishi in 1161. In the defence of Xiangyang against the Mongols from 1268 to 1273, Chinese military engineering was at its most resourceful. The two great military crises, the fall of Kaifeng (1127) and the Mongol conquest (1235–1279), both came about because the Song could not defeat mounted steppe armies that could manoeuvre around fixed defensive lines. The final naval battle at Yamen in 1279 showed that even strong naval resistance could not save the dynasty once the landward defences had fallen.
fields.governance: The Song state had the most developed bureaucracy of the medieval world. It rested on a civil service examination system that selected officials through rigorous written tests in the classics, literature and statecraft. The examinations, greatly expanded under Taizong and his successors, opened a real path to office by merit and produced a literate governing class drawn from a far wider social base than the hereditary aristocracy of earlier dynasties. Central government was divided between three bodies, the Secretariat-Chancellery for civil administration, the Bureau of Military Affairs and the Finance Commission. Their jurisdictions overlapped by design, so that no single official could accumulate excessive power. The Censorate independently monitored official conduct, investigated corruption and remonstrated with the emperor on matters of government. At the dynasty's height the bureaucracy numbered some 20,000 or more ranked officials, supported by a much larger body of clerks and subordinate staff. Wang Anshi's New Policies (1069–1076) were the most ambitious attempt to restructure Song government. They included the green sprouts loans (qingmiao fa), which gave peasants state credit to protect them from private moneylenders, the hired service system, which replaced labour conscription with cash payments, and military reorganisation. The reforms were reversed after Emperor Shenzong's death in 1085, one episode in the bitter factional struggle between reformers and conservatives that consumed much political energy through the late Northern Song. The Southern Song government operated under near-permanent military emergency. It kept enough fiscal discipline to fund prolonged resistance while sustaining the commercial economy whose tax revenues paid for that resistance.
fields.impact: The Song Dynasty's effect on world history was greater than its political power, and came mainly through the technology and commerce it developed and passed on. Three inventions of great consequence for later world history, gunpowder weapons, the magnetic compass and movable type printing, all reached mature or newly applied forms during the Song period. Bi Sheng invented movable type with ceramic characters around 1040 CE, four centuries before Gutenberg's press, although woodblock printing remained dominant in China, and the Song printing boom produced books on a scale unmatched elsewhere in the world. The magnetic compass, described by Shen Kuo in 1088 and recorded in use for maritime navigation by the early twelfth century, later reached Islamic and European navigators and eventually contributed to the European voyages of the Age of Discovery. Song maritime trade provided the commercial foundations of the maritime Silk Road. Song ceramics found at archaeological sites from Japan to East Africa and the Persian Gulf show how far that trade reached, and Chinese demand stimulated production in the Southeast and South Asian economies that supplied Chinese merchant ships. The Southern Song resisted the Mongols for more than four decades, longer than any other major state held out against Mongol expansion, and the gunpowder weapons refined during this struggle spread with the Mongols across Eurasia. The Neo-Confucian synthesis of Zhu Xi became the orthodox basis of the civil service examinations from 1313 and guided East Asian government and social organisation for the following six centuries.
fields.decline: The Song Dynasty fell to Mongol military power, which was of a scale and operational skill that no contemporary Asian state could withstand, and the Song's own military disadvantages made matters worse. War with the Mongols began in 1235 under the Great Khan Ögedei and continued under Möngke, who died while campaigning in Sichuan in 1259, and finally Kublai Khan. It took more than four decades to conquer a dynasty that defended itself with fortified cities, river fleets and the deep resources of southern China's rice economy. The siege of Xiangyang (1268–1273) was the decisive confrontation. The twin cities of Xiangyang and Fancheng on the Han River guarded the route to the Yangtze valley and the Southern Song heartland. They held out for five years and fell only after Kublai brought in engineers from the Ilkhanate whose counterweight trebuchets outranged the defenders' catapults. The siege showed Song tenacity and also the limits of static fortification against a besieger able to commit very large resources. The fall of Xiangyang opened the Yangtze, and resistance then collapsed quickly: the Mongol general Bayan routed the main Song army and fleet at the Battle of Dingjiazhou in 1275, and in 1276 Lin'an surrendered and the boy emperor Gong was taken north, while loyalists fled south with his younger brothers. The dynasty ended with the naval battle at Yamen in March 1279. A loyalist fleet of more than a thousand ships was destroyed, and the minister Lu Xiufu leapt into the sea carrying the last Song emperor, the seven-year-old Zhao Bing; many officials followed them. The fall was complete, in contrast to the administration and commerce the Song had sustained for over three centuries.
fields.summary: The Song Dynasty matters chiefly for the technology and commerce it developed: gunpowder weapons, the navigational compass, paper money and movable type, all of which later changed the world. Its influence spread through commerce and invention rather than conquest.
fields.teaser: The Song Dynasty introduced the first government-issued paper money, movable-type printing, gunpowder weapons and the magnetic compass at sea, and had one of China's most refined cultures.
fields.t0: The Song Dynasty ruled China from 960 to 1279, governed by exam-selected scholar-officials rather than generals.
fields.t1: It ran the world's most commercial economy, with paper money and huge cities, and developed gunpowder weapons, the compass and movable type.
fields.t2: Lacking warhorses and cavalry, it lost the north to the Jurchen in 1127 and fell to Kublai Khan's Mongols after four decades of resistance.
fields.dyk: Bi Sheng invented movable type using ceramic characters around 1040, some four centuries before Gutenberg's printing press.
